To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the microglial cell is a resident cell of the CNS which is capable of responding to a variety of threats in the CNS, such as trauma, infection, ischaemia or degeneration, and which is capable of performing different roles in the brain depending on the type of threat.
the microglial response is a graded one and that the microglia are a sensor to threats to the nervous system.

(i) microglia are derived from a bone-marrow precursor cell and settle the CNS antnatally and (ii) microglia can respond to CNS injury with a graded response, ranging from proliferation and migration to activation and phagocytosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of microglial cells, the immune cells of the brain.
(i) the development of microglia in normal and pathological CNS, (ii) the role of microglia as a sensor to CNS injury and (iii) the mechanisms involved in microglial proliferation.
the role of microglia in CNS injury and disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
microglia have been shown to be the first cell type in the CNS to react to any kind of insult and, therefore, may be a sensor to threats to the nervous system.
the microglial response is a key cellular event in CNS pathology.
the microglial response is an important part of the host defence mechanism in the CNS, and a key cellular response to many pathological conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microglia may be the first cell type in the CNS to sense the threat of injury and to respond to it.
microglia can act as a sensor of threats in the nervous tissue, and that the activation of microglia is a key event in the development of neuropathological conditions.
microglial activation is the first step in a chain of events leading to neuronal death.
The main takeaway from our work is that
microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, are not only the first responders to injury, but are also the first responders in the fight against infection in the brain.
microglia, which are normally a part of the immune system of the central nervous system (CNS) are activated in the brain of patients with HIV infection.
microglia have the ability to sense threats to the CNS, and that this ability may be important in a variety of conditions.
